facts.summary: Texas sets its state minimum wage equal to the federal minimum wage under the FLSA, so it is currently $7.25 per hour.
facts.notes: Section 62.051 expressly pegs the Texas minimum wage to the federal rate under Section 6, FLSA (29 U.S.C. 206). Figure moves automatically with the federal rate; verify the federal rate is still $7.25.

facts.summary: Texas has no state overtime or daily-overtime law and no higher salary floor; overtime is governed entirely by the federal FLSA.
facts.notes: Texas has no separate overtime statute. Section 62.151 excludes FLSA-covered persons from the state wage chapter, leaving FLSA's 40-hour/week overtime and salary-level rules to control.

facts.summary: Under the Texas Payday Law, an employee must file a wage claim with the Texas Workforce Commission no later than the 180th day after the wages became due for payment.
facts.notes: The 180-day deadline is jurisdictional under the statute. This is the administrative TWC claim route; a separate 2-year limitations period applies to civil minimum-wage recovery actions (see final-pay fact).

facts.summary: A civil action to recover unpaid minimum wages plus liquidated damages under the Texas Minimum Wage Act must be brought within two years of when the wages were due and payable.
facts.notes: Applies to the private civil action for minimum-wage violations (Section 62.201 liability), distinct from the 180-day TWC Payday Law claim.

value: sex (including pregnancy, childbirth, and related medical conditions)
facts.summary: The Texas Commission on Human Rights Act bars employment discrimination on the same bases as federal law, consolidated into one state statute, with pregnancy expressly included within sex.
facts.notes: Mirrors the federal protected-class set (Title VII, ADA, ADEA). Age protection is limited to individuals 40+; pregnancy is included in sex under Section 21.106.

facts.value: 15 employees (general); age discrimination reaches employers with 15+ (broader than the federal ADEA's 20-employee floor); public employers covered regardless of size
facts.summary: The TCHRA generally covers employers with 15 or more employees, but because age claims fall under the same 15-employee threshold, Texas reaches smaller employers for age discrimination than the federal ADEA.
facts.notes: Employer definition: 15+ employees for 20+ calendar weeks. Counties, municipalities, and state agencies/instrumentalities are covered regardless of employee count. Sexual harassment claims use a much broader definition (see sexual-harassment fact).

facts.value: All employers with one or more employees; prompt corrective-action duty
facts.summary: A 2021 Texas amendment makes sexual harassment an unlawful employment practice for every employer with at least one employee, and requires immediate and appropriate corrective action once harassment is known or should be known.
facts.notes: Added by Acts 2021, 87th Leg., S.B. 45. This is a Texas addition beyond federal Title VII's 15-employee floor; the filing deadline for sexual harassment complaints is also extended to 300 days (see discrimination-complaint deadline fact).

facts.summary: A discrimination complaint under the TCHRA must be filed with the TWC Civil Rights Division within 180 days of the alleged unlawful practice, extended to 300 days for sexual harassment complaints.
facts.notes: State FEPA (TWC Civil Rights Division) deadline is 180 days, shorter than the 300-day federal EEOC deadline that applies in Texas as a deferral state. The commission must dismiss untimely complaints.

facts.value: Reasonable accommodation required; good-faith effort defense codified
facts.summary: Texas law independently requires covered employers to make reasonable workplace accommodations for a known disability of a qualified individual unless it imposes undue hardship.
facts.notes: Parallels the federal ADA accommodation duty but is enforceable under state law through the TCHRA; Section 21.128 also provides a good-faith-effort defense to damages.

facts.value: Prohibited under TCHRA (opposition and participation activity)
facts.summary: The TCHRA makes it an unlawful employment practice to retaliate against a person who opposes discrimination, files a charge or complaint, or participates in an investigation or proceeding.
facts.notes: State-law analog to Title VII retaliation, enforced through the same TCHRA complaint process and deadlines.

facts.value: Public employees only; 90-day deadline to sue
facts.summary: The Texas Whistleblower Act protects public employees who in good faith report a legal violation by their governmental employer to an appropriate law enforcement authority, and requires suit within 90 days.
facts.notes: Applies only to state and local government employees, not private-sector employees. The 90-day limitation runs from when the violation occurred or was discovered through reasonable diligence.
